dialogue.scene: Reem and her cousin Lina are discussing Reem's idea of taking a gap year before starting university.

p1.t: So, are you seriously planning to take a year off before university?
I'm thinking about it. I'd volunteer and do an online design course. It would really broaden my horizons.
Granted, you'd gain experience, but don't you think you might lose momentum?
Admittedly, that's a risk. Getting back into studying after a long break isn't easy.
So how would you stop that from happening?
I'd keep a study routine, maybe two hours of maths a week, so I don't forget everything I learnt at school.

p2.t: And what about the cost? Your parents might see it as a wasted year.
That's a valid concern. That said, most of my plans are free or very cheap.
Fair enough. Just make sure you have a clear plan for every month.
I will. A gap year only works if it has a real purpose.
Have you talked to anyone who actually did one?

0-1.warmup: How often do you buy new clothes, and what makes you choose one shop over another?

dialogue.scene: Sara and Noura are preparing a short talk for their school's environment club about fast fashion.

p1.t: Fast fashion is a disaster. These brands cut corners everywhere to keep prices low.
I agree with you up to a point. It's true that quality is poor, but not everyone can afford expensive clothes.
Granted, but cheap clothes fall apart quickly, so people end up buying more.
That's fair. We're all partly to blame; we've become part of a throwaway culture.
Exactly. My cousin bought ten T-shirts last summer and threw most of them away by winter.
I've done the same, honestly. When something costs twenty riyals, you don't think twice about replacing it.

p2.t: And the low prices come at the expense of factory workers and the environment.
Admittedly, the environmental cost is huge. Some brands are trying to improve, though.
Up to a point. A small recycled collection doesn't change the whole business model.
So in our talk, let's suggest buying less, rather than never buying cheap clothes.
Fair enough. Maybe we can end with a challenge: no new clothes for a month.
Good idea, as long as we admit it'll be harder for some people than for others.

dialogue.focus: It's true that quality is poor, but not everyone can afford expensive clothes.

p1.t: The café pays well, and I'd get hands-on experience with real customers.
I take your point, but this is your final year. Can you really juggle a job and exams?
It's only weekends. In most cases, students who work learn to manage their time better.

dialogue.scene: Omar and his friend Daniel, an exchange student, are discussing the rapid growth of tourism on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast.

p1.t: The new resorts on the Red Sea look amazing. They must boost the local economy.
They do, but tourism can be a mixed blessing. Large resorts can put a strain on fragile coral reefs.
I'll grant you that, but aren't many of the projects designed to protect the environment?
Some are, yes. There's no denying that the plans are ambitious, but we'll only know the impact in a few years.
That's fair. Back home in England, some seaside towns became so crowded that local families moved away.
That's exactly my worry. A place can lose its character if it's built only for visitors.

p2.t: What about local people? Do they actually benefit?
Admittedly, there are new jobs. That said, rents and food prices can rise too; you have to take the rough with the smooth.
So overall, are you for it or against it?
On balance, I'm for it, as long as growth is carefully managed.
What would 'carefully managed' actually mean in practice?
Limits on visitor numbers, training local people for the new jobs, and protecting the reefs before building, not after.

p1.t: Much as I love football, I think these salaries are out of all proportion. A nurse earns a tiny fraction of that.
I'll grant you that. But star players generate revenue through tickets, TV rights and shirt sales.
Be that as it may, nobody needs that much money for kicking a ball.
Their careers are short, though. Many retire before thirty-five.
True, and injuries can end a career overnight. I hadn't really thought about that.
Exactly. A doctor can work until sixty-five, but a footballer might be finished at thirty after one bad tackle.

p2.t: Admittedly, a short career is a fair point. Even so, the gap with other jobs is shocking.
Big salaries are fine, within reason. What matters more is how players behave.
You mean because they're an inspiration to young people?
Exactly. A player who's a true inspiration to children is worth the money.
So you'd pay players well, but expect them to behave well in return?
Yes. That said, I'd also like clubs to spend more on youth academies, not just on stars.

dialogue.scene: Lama is practising a balanced talk for her English class on the question 'Should every student learn to code?'. Her friend Reem is listening and asking questions.

p1.t: Let me look at both sides. The case for coding is clear: it teaches logic, and many future jobs will need it.
Fine, but some students find it really hard. What would you say to them?
Admittedly, coding can be frustrating at first. That said, the basics are within everyone's reach.
Even so, isn't it unfair to give low marks to students who just don't think that way?
I must admit that it could be. That's why I'd grade effort and projects, not just tests.
So you'd make it compulsory for everyone until graduation?

p2.t: No. Don't get me wrong: coding isn't more important than art. Nevertheless, a basic level is essential today.
I take your point. So what's your conclusion?
For my money, one year of compulsory coding is fair. After that, students should choose.
That's a balanced argument. It concedes the problems but still takes a clear position.
Thanks. I'll finish by asking the class what they think, so it doesn't sound like a lecture.

dialogue.scene: Hamad's younger cousin Sara asks him how the water in their tap in Jeddah can come from the sea.

p1.t: Our teacher said our water comes from the sea. But seawater is salty! How does that work?
Good question. Saudi Arabia has very few rivers. What this means is that we rely heavily on desalination.
Desali-what? That word is far too long.
To put it simply, desalination means taking the salt out of seawater. Huge plants turn seawater into drinking water.
So those huge buildings on the coast near Jubail are desalination plants?
Exactly. Some of the biggest in the world are here, and they supply water to cities hundreds of kilometres inland.

p2.t: But how do they actually remove the salt?
Most plants push the water through extremely fine filters. In other words, the water gets through, but the salt doesn't.
That sounds easy. Why don't all countries do it?
Because it uses a vast amount of energy, so it's expensive. That's why we shouldn't waste water.
So every time I leave the tap running, I'm wasting energy as well as water?
That's right. Turning off the tap while you brush your teeth actually saves electricity, too.

dialogue.focus: To put it simply, desalination means taking the salt out of seawater.

p1.t: This chocolate bar used to cost two riyals. Now it's three! The shop is cheating.
Not really. It's called inflation. The long and short of it is that prices slowly go up over time.
But why does that matter? I've still got my two riyals.
Think of it as your money getting weaker. Put another way, the same two riyals buy less than before.
Weaker? But it's the same coin. It hasn't changed at all.
The coin is the same, but what it can buy has changed. Remember when two riyals bought a juice as well?

p2.t: So my money has less... power?
Exactly! Economists call it purchasing power. If prices rise and your pocket money doesn't keep up with them, you can buy less.
Then I need Dad to give me more pocket money!
Nice try. To put it simply, saving and spending wisely matter even more. Does that make sense?
Sort of. So if I keep my riyals in a box for years, they slowly lose value?
Yes. That's why grown-ups try to save in ways that grow over time, not just under the bed.

dialogue.scene: During a family dinner, Grandpa Saleh asks his grandson Majed how a phone app can recognise plants from a photo.

p1.t: Majed, how does this app know that the plant on the roof is mint? Is someone looking at my photos?
No, Grandpa. Essentially, it's artificial intelligence. It has learnt from millions of examples.
Learnt? A machine can't learn. It's just a machine.
A good analogy would be a child with a picture book. After seeing lots of mint leaves, the child recognises mint.
Like your little cousin learning the names of animals from her picture book?
Exactly. Except the machine needs millions of pictures, while my cousin needed only a few.

p2.t: So someone shows the machine pictures?
Engineers feed millions of labelled photos into it. That is to say, each photo comes with the plant's name.
And then it remembers them all?
Not exactly. By trial and error, it learns to spot patterns, like leaf shape. To put it simply, it makes a very good guess.
And does it ever get it wrong?
Sometimes. If it has never seen a plant before, it might confuse it with a similar one, so always double-check before you eat anything!

p1.t: Mona, the students keep saying 'Al-sabr miftah al-faraj'. What does it mean?

dialogue.scene: Ahmed has read an article for his biology class about the placebo effect. His friend Khalid finds the idea confusing.

p1.t: I read your article, but I couldn't make sense of it. What's a placebo?
The word 'placebo' refers to a fake treatment, like a sugar pill with no medicine in it.
So why would a doctor give someone a fake pill?
Usually only in experiments. The idea behind it is to compare it with the real medicine.
So in the experiment, nobody knows whether they've got the real pill or the fake one?
Exactly. Otherwise, people's expectations would affect the results, and the comparison wouldn't be fair.

p2.t: And the strange part is that people actually feel better?
Some do. In layman's terms, believing you'll get better can sometimes help your body a little.
So the sugar pill cures you?
No. Let me rephrase that. The pill does nothing; your expectations do. It's a bit like mind over matter.
That's fascinating. So should doctors give fake pills to make people feel better?
No, that wouldn't be honest. But it does show how much our thoughts can affect our bodies.

p1.t: The Riyadh Metro trains have no driver. To put it simply, the train drives itself. Let me break it down into three parts.
First, sensors on the track tell the system where every train is. Second, a control centre tracks all the trains in real time.
Third, computers control the speed and the doors. What this means is that trains can run safely close together.

dialogue.scene: Rakan and Liam are preparing a presentation on desertification for their geography class.

p1.t: So what actually causes desertification? Is it just the hot weather?
Not only that. In many areas, it stems from human activity, especially overgrazing and cutting down trees.
How does overgrazing make things worse?
Animals eat all the plants, so the soil is left bare. Bare soil can give rise to more sand and dust storms.
I didn't realise dust storms were partly caused by people.
Not all of them, of course, but bare ground makes them more frequent and much worse.

p2.t: And I suppose that has a domino effect on wildlife and farming.
Exactly. Fewer plants mean fewer animals and poorer harvests. This has led to big plans for planting native trees.
Do you think we can really reverse the trend?
To some extent, yes, if we choose plants that need little water and protect the areas we plant.
Which plants would work best here?
Native trees like ghaf and acacia. Their deep roots find water underground, so they survive long, dry summers.
Then let's end our presentation with that: a problem people caused, and a solution people can lead.

dialogue.scene: On a school trip to a beach near Yanbu, marine biology student Dana explains plastic pollution to a group of students. Ziyad asks questions.

p1.t: Why is there so much plastic on this beach? Nobody lives near here.
Most of it comes from elsewhere. Plastic from cities and ships often ends up in the sea, and currents carry it here.
And is it really that harmful? It's just rubbish.
It poses a threat to almost all sea life. Turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish and swallow them.
That's awful. Can't they tell the difference?
Not easily. In the water, a floating bag moves just like a jellyfish, and turtles have eaten jellyfish for millions of years.

p2.t: What about the coral reefs? Are they affected, too?
Yes. Plastic can carry disease to coral, and stress from pollution and warmer water can trigger bleaching.
So damaged reefs mean fewer fish?
Exactly, and that sets off a chain reaction: fishermen, in turn, lose their income. Some damage may be irreversible.
So what can we actually do, apart from picking up rubbish today?
Use fewer single-use bottles and support clean-up groups. Small habits, repeated by millions, really add up.

p1.t: In our example, the fake message saying a popular brand of bottled water was unsafe was doing the rounds in less than an hour.
Because nobody checked it. Wanting to be the first to share is at the root of the problem.
And exciting news fuels the sharing. People forward it before they think.
In the example, it gave rise to real confusion. Some families threw away bottles that were perfectly safe.
So one message managed to sow confusion across a whole town.

Then our solution should be simple: check the source before you share.

p1.t: Nawaf, what are the underlying causes of young people becoming less active?
Hot summers play a part, but the main driving force behind it is time spent sitting: at desks, in cars and on screens.
Sami, why should we be worried?
Inactivity has far-reaching consequences. It can result in obesity and diabetes, and it contributes to stress and poor sleep.

p1.t: How do people in your country usually measure success?
Nine times out of ten, people look at your job and your income. Climbing the career ladder is seen as a sign of success.
Do you think that's the right way to measure it?
Only partly. There's more to life than a job title. My grandmother never worked in an office, but she's the most respected person I know.
Why is she so respected?
She raised six children, helped half the neighbourhood and always had time to listen. Nobody ever asked about her salary.

p2.t: So what does happiness depend on, in your view?
I think it boils down to two things: strong relationships and peace of mind.
That's interesting. Why peace of mind rather than excitement or adventure?
Because excitement fades quickly, whereas feeling secure lets you enjoy everything else.

Achievement matters, admittedly. Helping others gives me a sense of fulfilment that no salary could.

More and more, I think. My friends talk about jobs they'll enjoy, not just jobs that pay well.

Mainly because they take years to master and don't pay well. Most teenagers would rather study something with a clear career path.

To some extent. My grandparents hold on to every custom, while my generation picks the ones that fit modern life.

Definitely. I think tradition and progress can go hand in hand. It's about getting the mix right, not choosing one side.
